grammar.title: Personal Pronouns
grammar.explanation: Personal pronouns are used to replace nouns. In German, 'ich' is 'I', 'du' is informal 'you', and 'Sie' is formal 'you'.

listening.audioText: Guten Morgen! Wie geht es dir?
listening.question: What time of day is it?

speaking.task: Introduce yourself.
speaking.prompt: Say: Hello, I am [Your Name].

speaking.task: Greet someone in the morning.
speaking.prompt: Say: Good morning!

roleplay.scenario: You meet a colleague for the first time.
roleplay.startingLine: Guten Morgen! Ich bin neu hier.

grammar.title: Verb Conjugation
grammar.explanation: Verbs in German change their endings depending on the subject. For 'ich' it usually ends in '-e', for 'du' it ends in '-st', and for 'er/sie/es' it ends in '-t'.

listening.audioText: Ich wohne in Berlin, aber ich komme aus Spanien.
listening.question: Where does the speaker live?

listening.audioText: Das ist Herr Schmidt. Er wohnt in Frankfurt.
listening.question: Where does Herr Schmidt live?

speaking.task: Tell someone where you live.
speaking.prompt: Say: I live in [City].

speaking.task: Ask someone where they come from (informal).
speaking.prompt: Say: Where do you come from?

roleplay.scenario: You are introducing yourself to a new neighbor.
roleplay.startingLine: Hallo! Ich wohne nebenan. Wie heißt du?

grammar.title: Questions & Age
grammar.explanation: To ask about age in German, use 'Wie alt...?' (How old...?). The verb 'sein' (to be) is used, just like in English.

speaking.task: Say your age.
speaking.prompt: Say: I am [your age] years old.

speaking.task: Ask someone for their phone number (informal).
speaking.prompt: Say: What is your phone number?

roleplay.scenario: You are filling out a form at a reception desk.
roleplay.startingLine: Guten Tag. Wie alt sind Sie und wie ist Ihre Telefonnummer?

listening.question: How many sisters does the speaker have?

speaking.task: Introduce your mother.
speaking.prompt: Say: This is my mother.

speaking.task: State how many siblings you have.
speaking.prompt: Say: I have [number] brothers and [number] sisters.

roleplay.scenario: You are showing a photo of your family to a friend.
roleplay.startingLine: Wer ist das auf dem Foto?

items.title: Level 1: Food & Drinks

grammar.title: Akkusativ
grammar.explanation: The direct object of a sentence takes the accusative case. Masculine 'ein' becomes 'einen' (einen Kaffee). Feminine 'eine' and neuter 'ein' stay the same.

listening.audioText: Ich möchte bitte einen Kaffee mit Milch.
listening.question: How does the speaker want their coffee?

listening.audioText: Trinkst du lieber Tee oder Kaffee?
listening.question: What is the speaker asking?
options: Do you prefer tea or coffee?
listening.answer: Do you prefer tea or coffee?

speaking.task: Order a coffee.
speaking.prompt: Say: I would like a coffee, please.

speaking.task: Say what you are eating.
speaking.prompt: Say: I am eating an apple.

roleplay.scenario: You are at a café ordering breakfast.
roleplay.startingLine: Guten Morgen! Was möchten Sie trinken?

items.review: You completed Level 1 of Food & Drinks!

items.title: Level 1: Time & Date

grammar.title: Word Order
grammar.explanation: In a German main clause, the conjugated verb is ALWAYS in the second position. If a time word (like 'heute') starts the sentence, the subject moves after the verb: 'Heute habe ich frei.'

practice.question: Morgen ___ wir ins Kino.
practice.translation: Tomorrow we are going to the cinema.

practice.question: Um acht Uhr ___ der Film.
practice.translation: At eight o'clock the film begins.

practice.question: Am Montag ___ sie arbeiten.
practice.translation: On Monday she has to work.

listening.question: Does the speaker have time today?

speaking.task: Say you have free time today.
speaking.prompt: Say: Today I have free time.

speaking.task: Say it is 3 o'clock.
speaking.prompt: Say: It is three o'clock.

roleplay.scenario: You are arranging a time to meet a friend.
roleplay.startingLine: Hast du heute Abend Zeit?

items.review: You completed Level 1 of Time & Date!

practice.translation: Excuse me, how do I get to the train station?

practice.question: ___ Sie die erste Straße rechts.
practice.translation: Take the first street on the right.

practice.question: Die Bank ___ auf der linken Seite.
practice.translation: The bank is on the left side.

listening.audioText: Gehen Sie geradeaus und dann die zweite Straße links.
listening.question: Where should you turn?

listening.audioText: Der Bahnhof ist in der Nähe.

speaking.task: Ask where the train station is.
speaking.prompt: Say: Excuse me, where is the train station?

speaking.task: Tell someone to go straight ahead.

grammar.title: haben vs. sein
grammar.explanation: Use 'sein' (to be) for states like 'Ich bin krank' (I am sick). Use 'haben' (to have) for symptoms like 'Ich habe Kopfschmerzen' (I have a headache).

practice.question: Sie ___ einen Termin beim Arzt.
practice.translation: She has an appointment at the doctor's.

listening.audioText: Ich habe seit zwei Tagen Halsschmerzen.
listening.question: How long has the patient had a sore throat?

speaking.task: Tell the doctor you have a headache.
speaking.prompt: Say: I have a headache.

speaking.task: Say that you are sick.
speaking.prompt: Say: I am sick.

roleplay.scenario: You are at the doctor's office describing your symptoms.
roleplay.startingLine: Guten Morgen. Ich bin leider krank.

items.title: Cultural Note
items.content: A quick tip to remember when practicing doctor in Germany!

grammar.title: haben vs. sein
grammar.explanation: Use 'sein' (to be) for states like 'Ich bin krank' (I am sick). Use 'haben' (to have) for symptoms like 'Ich habe Kopfschmerzen' (I have a headache).
